scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Two paths are not always enough. Today we build a ladder of conditions, and learn why the order matters.

scenes.onScreen: "More than two paths": three numbered lines (1. elif adds more conditions; 2. Python checks from the top; 3. The first True condition wins and the rest are skipped) and an analogy card: a ladder: you start at the top rung and step down until one rung holds your weight
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Sometimes there are many paths. Grade A, B, C and D. Python handles them with elif, short for else if. It checks the conditions from the top. The first one that is True wins, and Python skips the rest. Think of a ladder. You start at the top rung and step down until one rung holds. Because the first True wins, the order of the rungs matters a lot.

lines: The first True condition wins and the rest are skipped

scenes.onScreen: grade.py: marks turned into a grade with elif
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Marks are seventy two. [HL 2] First rung. Is it ninety or more? No. [HL 3] So Grade A is skipped. [HL 4] Second rung. Seventy five or more? No, seventy two is smaller. [HL 5] Skipped. [HL 6] Third rung. Sixty or more? Yes. [HL 7] So Grade C prints. [HL 8] Python never looks at else. [HL 9] That last line is a safety net for everything below sixty.

scenes.onScreen: Two tags, age and price, tied to an int each
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Look at the end state. Age is tied to the int sixty five. Price is tied to the int seventy. Only one of the four branches ran, and only that branch tied the name price to a value. If no branch runs, the name price does not exist. That is why we added a final else.

scenes.onScreen: ticket.py: a ticket price chosen by age
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] [TRACK age=65] Age is sixty five. [HL 2] Under five? No. [HL 4] Under eighteen? No. [HL 6] Under sixty? No. [HL 8] Everything else lands in else, so the price is seventy, a senior discount. [HL 10] Print the chosen price. Notice that every branch ties the same name, price. That way the last line always has a price to print.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as ticket dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, ticket dot py. Ticket price, seventy.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: elif adds more conditions after if. Two: Python checks from the top and runs only the first True branch. Three: Order matters: put the strictest condition first. Four: A final else catches everything that is left. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: conditions in the wrong order
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Marks are ninety five, a perfect grade A. But the program prints Grade C. Why? The first rung is, sixty or more. Ninety five passes it, and Python stops right there. The ninety test is never reached. Put the strictest condition first, and work down to the loosest.

props.why: Python stops at the first True condition, so a loose test placed first hides every stricter test below it.

shorts.title: What is elif?
shorts.script: Elif is short for else if. It lets you add more conditions after the first if. Python checks them from the top, and runs the first branch whose condition is True. Then it skips everything else in the ladder. So exactly one branch runs. Think of climbing down a ladder until a rung holds your weight. Use elif whenever you have three or more choices. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A ladder of conditions.

shorts.title: First True wins
shorts.hook: "Here is the golden rule of the elif ladder."
shorts.script: Here is the golden rule of the elif ladder. Python stops at the first True condition. Marks are seventy two. Is it ninety or more? No. Seventy five or more? No. Sixty or more? Yes, so Grade C prints, and Python never looks at the rest. Only one branch runs, no matter how many conditions could be true. Remember this rule. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Only one branch runs.

shorts.title: The last else
shorts.script: End your ladder with an else. It catches everything that no condition matched. Without it, a value that fails every test runs nothing. Later lines can then use a name that does not exist. A final else is your safety net. Even a simple message like, invalid input, is better than silence. Add one every time. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Catch everything left.

shorts.title: Wrong order, wrong grade
shorts.script: Here is a sneaky bug. Marks are ninety five, but the program prints Grade C. The first rung says, sixty or more. Ninety five passes that, so Python stops, and never reaches the ninety test. There is no error, only a wrong answer. Put the strictest condition first, and then work down to the loosest one. Test with a perfect score. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Order the rungs.

shorts.script: Why did the elif ladder get a promotion? It was always one step ahead. Your challenge. Make temp equal twenty four. Print Cold if it is below fifteen. Print Warm if it is below thirty. Otherwise print Hot. Remember to put the strictest condition first. Then test fourteen, thirty, and forty. Post your code in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 14.
